From organic waste to cooking gas

Lenkai Enterprises Limited develops waste-to-energy projects in Arusha, Tanzania. Our focus is biogas for kitchens and productive uses for the organic material left after digestion.

ARUSHA, TANZANIA/ESTABLISHED 2023

COMPANY OVERVIEW

About Lenkai

We are a Tanzanian project developer working at the intersection of organic waste management and cooking energy. We bring waste producers, kitchen operators and engineers together to assess where local biogas supply can work.

Our mission

Develop commercially viable projects that turn suitable organic waste into cooking gas and recover useful agricultural resources.

Our vision

Build an East African network of circular-economy projects, beginning with a viable waste-to-energy and clean cooking hub in Arusha.

LEADERSHIP

A message from the CEO

Priscilla Joseph Mollel

Chief Executive Officer

Our starting point in Arusha is a practical question. Can the organic material that markets, farms and kitchens discard each day supply cooking fuel that customers can count on?

A useful answer starts with the people who will run and use the system. A market operator needs a reliable collection schedule. A school kitchen needs fuel when meals are due. A farmer needs to know whether the material left after digestion is suitable for the land. Each decision shapes the design.

We are assessing an integrated hub in Arusha and preparing a cylinder distribution system that could reach kitchens beyond a direct gas line. Our immediate priorities are to understand available feedstocks, agree how gas quality will be checked and establish the costs of delivering fuel to customers.

Our invitation

We welcome waste suppliers, cooking-energy customers and implementation partners who can help us test the case for a first site.

OUR SERVICES

Services for organisations

Schools, hospitals, hotels and food businesses often know when their kitchens run and how much fuel they buy. These records give us a basis for assessing biogas demand and designing a supply arrangement.

Institutional scale

The pictured 54 m³ digester illustrates the civil works behind a medium-scale system. Site conditions, available organic material and kitchen demand determine the size appropriate for each project.

For kitchen operators

The assessment starts with fuel purchases, meal schedules and peak cooking periods. These inputs inform burner compatibility, supply volume, delivery frequency and continuity of service.

For waste generators

Markets, farms and food processors can contribute volumes, seasonal patterns and collection constraints. These determine the material a digester can accept and the cost of keeping it supplied.

For host institutions

Where a kitchen and digester can share a site, we assess direct supply. Where distance matters, cylinder delivery can be evaluated against transport costs, storage needs and expected demand.

OUR SERVICES

Biogas for farms and households

A small digester can use a steady stream of suitable organic material close to the kitchen. The practical questions are how much feedstock is available each day, who will operate the unit and when the gas is needed.

Choosing a system for daily use

For a livestock farm, the starting point is a realistic manure collection routine and enough space for digestion and slurry handling. For a household, the assessment also considers access to water, usable space, burner type and the amount of time the household can devote to daily operation.

Where a kitchen cannot host a digester, a delivered cylinder could offer another route to biogas. Household service would depend on affordable refills, compatible appliances, reliable returns and the availability of trained local support.

What a first assessment needs

Typical daily feedstock, the existing cooking fuel, the hours of use, available space and the person responsible for operating the system.

FLAGSHIP PROJECT

The proposed Arusha hub

The Lenkai Integrated Organic Waste-to-Energy and Clean Cooking Hub would bring local waste treatment and fuel supply together at one facility. The project is in concept development and feasibility assessment.

The first market

Institutional and commercial kitchens are the initial focus. Their cooking schedules and purchase records can establish the demand needed to size the facility and assess a supply agreement.

What would move through the hub

Organic inputs

Potential feedstocks include market produce waste, food-processing residues, kitchen waste and livestock manure. A waste audit will establish the usable quantities, composition and seasonal variation.

Biogas production

The proposed plant would inspect and prepare incoming material before anaerobic digestion. It would condition the recovered gas to meet the needs of the selected storage and cooking equipment.

Customer supply

Nearby kitchens could take gas through a dedicated connection. Cylinder delivery would be assessed for customers beyond practical piping distance.

Material recovery

Digestate could have agricultural value where treatment, testing and local land-use requirements support it. The study will also account for residues that require disposal.

Feasibility decisions

Site selection, plant capacity, the feedstock mix and capital costs will follow from the waste audit, engineering design, customer demand and financing terms.

HOW IT WORKS

Direct biogas supply

A kitchen close to a digester can use conditioned biogas through a dedicated gas line. The short route can suit a farm, a school kitchen or another user with regular on-site demand.

From digestion to use

Anaerobic digestion converts suitable organic material into biogas. The gas line carries it towards the kitchen. Moisture removal and treatment, including hydrogen sulphide removal where required, help match the gas to the intended appliance.

Where it fits

On-site users with predictable cooking loads, a practical pipe route and a dependable supply of feedstock.

What to establish

Gas demand at peak hours, the quality required at the appliance and the capacity for ongoing operation and maintenance.

NEW BUSINESS LINE

ANG cylinder distribution

Lenkai has completed development of its proposed adsorbed natural gas (ANG) cylinder system for cooking-fuel distribution. The system is awaiting execution.

How adsorption supports delivery

An ANG cylinder contains a porous adsorbent that holds methane on its internal surface. Gas can be released through a regulated outlet for use in a compatible appliance. The proposed service would move conditioned gas from a production site to kitchens in exchangeable cylinders.

The service to be implemented

A filling point would prepare cylinders for dispatch. Customers would receive filled units and return empties for inspection and refill. Delivery routes and exchange intervals would be matched to actual cooking demand.

HOW IT WORKS

How the cylinder system works

The cylinder route adds storage, filling and transport to the direct-supply model. The receiving kitchen needs a compatible cylinder connection, regulator and appliance.

Condition and buffer

Buffer storage balances gas production and filling demand. The process must meet the gas-quality specification for the selected adsorbent, cylinder and end use.

Fill and distribute

The design links treatment, metering, compression and a filling manifold. The operating plan will define inspection, tracking and return arrangements for each cylinder.

Execute and verify

Implementation priorities include site readiness, vendor validation, applicable approvals, operator training and commissioning checks before customer supply.

HOW WE WORK

Project delivery and performance

Lenkai’s roadmap begins with a local feasibility case. Expansion depends on operating evidence from the first project and demand for the same service elsewhere.

01

Feasibility and project preparation

Audit the waste available, map collection distances, measure customer fuel use and compare site and technology options. The result is a proposed facility size, delivery model and investment case.

02

Financing and implementation

Agree feedstock and gas supply terms, secure financing and required approvals, complete engineering and procurement, and commission the first facility.

03

Operating review and expansion

Use delivery records, maintenance costs and customer demand to improve service. Those results will guide decisions about additional customers, routes or sites.

What we intend to measure

Waste and energy

Record accepted feedstock, contamination, usable gas produced and gas delivered.

Cooking and climate

Compare customers’ fuel use with a documented baseline. Track methane losses, fuel displacement and emissions assumptions before estimating climate benefits.

Operations and safety

Track equipment checks, gas quality, cylinder movements, operator training and incidents. Test digestate before considering agricultural use.

COMMERCIAL DEVELOPMENT

Partnerships and investment

The proposed hub needs a reliable supply of suitable waste and customers willing to buy the resulting cooking fuel. Agreements on volumes and prices will shape the engineering and financial model.

Waste and site partners

Municipalities, market operators, farms and processors can help establish available quantities, collection schedules, contamination levels and access to suitable sites.

Energy customers

Hotels, restaurants, schools and hospitals can share fuel purchases, peak cooking periods and site constraints. The next step is to compare the delivered cost and practicality of direct supply and cylinder service.

Engineering partners

Digester designers, gas-treatment specialists, cylinder and appliance suppliers, and local service providers can assess equipment compatibility, commissioning needs and maintenance support.

Finance partners

The company is exploring promoter equity, development finance, technical assistance and grants for eligible preparation work. Funding structure will depend on feasibility, investment risk and agreed commercial terms.

What the business case will test

Potential income includes gas sales and contracted waste-treatment fees. Digestate sales depend on product quality and demand. Any carbon revenue would require an eligible methodology, monitoring, independent verification and a market.

Our values in practice

We value responsible use of local resources, safety for the people who handle gas and affordability for the people who cook with it. We assess each project against those commitments before deciding how to invest.
